findings.title: Shutdown discards unprocessed items still in the queue
findings.body: In `OrderedQueueWorker.run()`, the loop condition is `while not self.shutdown`. When `FixedQueuePool.shutdown()` sets `worker.shutdown = True`, the worker will finish its current item and then exit the loop without draining remaining items from the queue. Even though `q.shutdown(immediate=False)` is called (which would allow `get()` to continue returning items until the queue is empty), the worker never reaches `get()` because the `while not self.shutdown` check fails first. Any items still queued will be silently lost and their offsets will never be marked complete, potentially blocking future offset commits for those partitions.

findings.title: Race condition iterating `all_offsets` keys while other threads add new partitions
findings.body: `get_committable_offsets()` calls `list(self.all_offsets.keys())` without holding any lock. Concurrently, `add_offset()` on a new partition triggers `defaultdict.__getitem__` which inserts a new key into `self.all_offsets`. In CPython, modifying a dict while another thread is iterating its keys (which `list(dict.keys())` does internally) can raise `RuntimeError: dictionary changed size during iteration`. This can crash the commit loop, preventing any further offset commits.

findings.title: Unbounded queues provide no backpressure, risking OOM under load
findings.body: `queue.Queue()` is created without a `maxsize`, making it unbounded. The class docstring claims 'Natural backpressure when queues fill up' but no backpressure mechanism exists. If messages arrive faster than workers can process them (e.g., during a downstream outage), queues grow without limit. The `submit()` method never raises `MessageRejected` (arroyo's backpressure signal), so the consumer will continue polling and submitting indefinitely. Consider setting a `maxsize` and raising `MessageRejected` from `submit()` when the queue is full.

findings.title: Failed messages are marked as complete and committed, preventing retry
findings.body: In `OrderedQueueWorker.run()`, the `finally` block calls `self.offset_tracker.complete_offset(...)` regardless of whether `result_processor` succeeded or raised an exception. This means messages that fail processing are still marked as done and their offsets will be committed. If processing fails due to a transient error (database timeout, network issue), the message is permanently lost with no retry. The error is only logged. Consider not completing the offset on failure, or implementing a retry/DLQ mechanism.

findings.title: AssertionError in submit() can cause offset to never be tracked, blocking partition commits
findings.body: In `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit()`, `assert isinstance(message.value, BrokerValue)` is used. If Python is run with optimizations (`-O` flag), assertions are stripped, and `message.value` might not be a `BrokerValue`. The subsequent access to `message.value.partition` would raise `AttributeError`, caught by the `except Exception` block. In the except block, `isinstance(message.value, BrokerValue)` would be False, so the offset is never added/completed. If this happens for a message whose offset was already added by a prior code path or expected by the offset tracker, it could create a gap that blocks all future commits for that partition. Use an explicit `isinstance` check with proper error handling instead of `assert`.

findings.title: Python's `hash()` is randomized across process restarts, weakening ordering guarantees after rebalance
findings.body: `get_queue_for_group` uses `hash(group_key) % self.num_queues`. Python's string hash is randomized per process (PYTHONHASHSEED). After a consumer restart or partition rebalance, the same group_key will likely map to a different queue index. While ordering within a single process lifetime is preserved, if there are any assumptions about consistent queue assignment across restarts (e.g., for debugging or metrics), this could be surprising. Consider using a stable hash like `hashlib.md5(group_key.encode()).hexdigest()` or `zlib.crc32` for deterministic assignment.

findings.title: `join()` calls `close()` which may be called twice in arroyo lifecycle
findings.body: Arroyo's `StreamProcessor` typically calls `close()` and then `join()` on a processing strategy during shutdown. Here, `join()` calls `self.close()` again, resulting in `close()` being invoked twice. The second invocation calls `self.queue_pool.shutdown()` on an already-shut-down pool and `self.commit_thread.join()` on an already-joined thread. While this is likely benign (join on a finished thread returns immediately), it's fragile and could mask issues if the shutdown logic becomes more complex. `join()` should only wait for completion, not re-trigger shutdown.

findings.title: Test asserts all 3 queues are used with only 20 groups, which is probabilistic
findings.body: `test_different_groups_distributed` asserts `len(queue_indices) == 3` for 20 group keys hashed into 3 queues. While very likely with Python's hash distribution, this is not guaranteed. If the hash function happens to map all 20 keys to fewer than 3 buckets (extremely unlikely but possible), the test would fail non-deterministically. A more robust approach would be to verify the property over a larger sample or use a deterministic hash in the test.
